stories.title: The Broken Ankle
stories.description: Ajay recounts the story of breaking his ankle on a hike. It happened not during a difficult climb, but on a descent from Tung fort when he relaxed his guard, thinking the hard part was over. They got lost, followed a pipe (a mistake), and he slipped. The lesson is to never relax until the tent is pitched.

stories.title: The Goecha La Decision
stories.description: Ajay shares a memory from his Goecha La trek in Sikkim. At Goecha La 1, despite being close to the next viewpoint (Goecha La 2), he decided to turn back because his fingers were freezing and hurting intensely. He reflects on the difficulty of making rational 'turn back' decisions in the mountains when suffering from the sunk cost fallacy or 'summit fever'.

stories.title: The First Ascent of Konkankada
stories.description: Ajay describes his role as a 'coolie' (porter) for the first successful climb of the Konkankada face of Harishchandragad by a team from IIT Bombay. He hauled supplies up and down the vertical face and rappelled down 1800 feet, spinning 360 degrees on the rope to take in the view.

stories.title: The Origins of Pedestrianism
stories.description: Amit tells the story of Edward Weston, who bet that Lincoln would lose the election. When Lincoln won, Weston walked from Boston to Washington. This feat sparked a craze called 'Pedestrianism', which became a massive spectator sport in the late 19th century, with stars like Dan O'Leary and Frank Hart competing in grueling six-day walking races.

stories.title: Petrosian Plays to Play
stories.description: Amit shares an anecdote about chess grandmaster Tigran Petrosian. During a game, an opponent asked if he was playing for a win or a draw. Petrosian replied, 'I'm playing to play.' This illustrates the ideal state of doing something for the pure love of the activity itself.

stories.title: Teenagers on Their Butts
stories.description: Ajay contrasts his own fitness with that of teenagers he accompanied on a trek to Panchachuli. He found the teenagers, who spent their lives 'sitting on their butts watching Netflix', to be shockingly unfit compared to the older generation.

core_ideas.description: Referencing E.O. Wilson, Ajay discusses 'biophilia' as the innate human tendency to seek connections with nature and other forms of life. He argues that humans are 'monkeys' meant to live amidst trees, not just in concrete jungles.

Amit quotes Dilip Chitre's poem about 'man's estrangement from a man-made world'. Ajay connects this to Marx's concept of alienation, suggesting that living purely urban lives leaves a 'hole in the heart'.

core_ideas.idea: The Sunk Cost Fallacy in Hiking
core_ideas.description: A critical danger in mountaineering is the sunk cost fallacy—refusing to turn back because of the effort already invested. Ajay emphasizes the need to be 'cold and rational' and make the decision to turn around if conditions (weather, health) demand it, regardless of how close the summit is.

Ajay's maxim: 'It is the fate of every great idea to start out as a movement, then become a business, and then become a racket.' This is applied to the commercialization of hiking and climbing (e.g., Everest tourism).
Ajay describes hiking not just as exercise but as a meditative zone where one becomes acutely aware of their body, breathing, and surroundings. It requires a 'shut up and do it' discipline.
A strong plea for hygiene in the mountains: don't litter, use cotton wet wipes (biodegradable) instead of plastic ones, and maintain silence (no Bluetooth speakers) to respect the sanctity of nature.

core_ideas.idea: Never Relax Until the Tent is Pitched
core_ideas.description: The lesson from Ajay's accident: accidents often happen when you think the hard work is done. Constant vigilance is required until the day is truly over.
